title: Taste, smell, hearing, and theories of vision (vol. II, pp. 16–18)
en:
If flavour is apprehended by actual particles mingling with saliva, the moisture acts as a mediator which conveys the sensible substance and its quality into contact with the tongue, and the sense directly encounters the flavoured substance. If saliva itself is changed into the appropriate taste, it is the altered moisture which the sense immediately encounters. Taste and touch may nevertheless be experienced together on the tongue. Sometimes the two sensations remain distinct, as with a thing that is both sweet and hot; sometimes they form one complex experience almost like a single flavour. Acridity combines a flavour with a divisive or irritating heating effect; acidity combines flavour with a divisive effect without heating; astringency joins flavour to drying or contracting action.

**Smell.** Most explain smelling by the arrival at the organ of smell of air transformed by the quality of the odorous object. A second school posits evaporation and separation of fine particles from the object which mingle with air and reach the organ. A third makes the odorous object act on the sensory organ without the intervening air receiving the odour-quality and without the object's exhaling particles. Against the particulate view it is said that a small amount of musk may be smelled for a long time in many places without observable loss of weight or size. Against the view of action without alteration of air it is said that musk can be carried far away or wholly burned, yet its odour persists in the originally affected air. Proponents of particles argue that heat, rubbing and evaporation intensify smells, severe cold conceals them and an apple reportedly withers after repeated smelling; these phenomena, they say, would be inexplicable without the emission of fine parts. One can deny the entailment: volatilisation might *assist* the air in receiving an odour-quality, while touching and repeated smelling could help dry and wither the apple in other ways. Those who reject the modified-air theory argue that even fire, powerful as it is in transforming adjacent bodies, does not heat beyond a certain distance; how can a fragrant body alter air many days' travel away? Aristotle is quoted as reporting vultures travelling for days toward the smell of corpses after a battle in a place where no such birds lived. The answer is that improbability does not establish impossibility; moreover strong winds might carry odorous air across great distances.

Claims are also reported, from Plato, Pythagoras, Hermes and others, that celestial bodies possess smell and fragrances. Peripatetics object that neither alterable air nor evaporated particles exist there. A reply confines those bodily requirements to the sublunary elements. Some later writers appeal to experiences in sleep or wakefulness of celestial fragrances surpassing musk and ambergris; practitioners of “spiritual sciences” are reported as attributing a particular incense to each star and a characteristic fragrance to each associated spirit, which supposedly enjoys the fragrance of prepared foods and rewards practitioners who arrange them. These are attributed claims, not endorsed facts.

**Hearing.** The account of sound in the earlier discussion supplies what is needed. The intermediate air is the undulating air conveying a sound whether it arises from striking (*qarʿ*) or separation (*qalʿ*). It is intermediate between the movement produced by the striking or separating bodies and the auditory cavity. The *Shifāʾ* describes the hearing faculty as situated in nerves spread over the inner surface of the ear, receiving the form conveyed by air violently compressed between a striker and a resisting struck body; its undulation reaches the stationary air enclosed in the auditory passage and sets it into motion. The difficulty in that wording is that it seems to mention only impact, though the author elsewhere explicitly allows separation as a source of sound.

Two objections are considered. First, how does undulating air preserve the determinate articulations and shapes of letters while entering narrow channels and striking solid walls? Second, if sound inheres in the entire mass of disturbed air, it should reach only one ear as a whole and only one listener hear it. If sound inheres in each constituent portion, each hearer should hear it repeatedly, as many times as portions of air reach the ear. The reply to these objections is introduced by an expression of possibility rather than an unqualified demonstration. If audible sound and its perception depend on air, the mere contact of celestial spheres could neither produce sound nor transmit it to us through an impenetrable celestial body. Yet ancient authorities are said to have attributed extraordinary sounds and harmonies to the heavens. Pythagoras is reported to have ascended in soul to the higher realm, heard the notes of the spheres through the purity of his soul, and subsequently arranged musical intervals and developed the art of music on returning to bodily faculties. The commentator reports rather than independently establishes this account.

**Vision.** On the anatomical scheme received by the commentators, seven pairs of nerves issue from the brain. The first pair begins deep within the anterior ventricles near two protrusions resembling nipples. These small hollow nerves pass across and intersect, so the nerve coming from the right passes to the left side and the one from the left to the right, reaching the respective pupils. That the perceptive powers inhabit these locations is argued from damage to them impairing the associated acts of perception.

Several accounts of sight are debated. The **impression theory** (*inṭibāʿ*) says that an image or likeness (*shabaḥ*) of the visible object is formed in the crystalline moisture of the eye, comparable to a mirror. When a coloured illuminated object confronts the receptive surface through a transparent medium, its image arises there, not because some portion of the object detaches and travels to the eye, but in the way a reflection occurs in a mirror. Two objections follow: on this account, it would appear that we see only the likeness rather than the thing itself, contrary to the direct certainty that we see the visible thing; and if the image must have the same magnitude as its object, a small crystalline body could not receive the image of something much larger. Replies are that seeing by an image need not make the *image* the object seen—what is seen is the thing whose image is impressed, as in the earlier discussion of knowledge—and that likeness demands correspondence of shape and colour, not equality of magnitude, just as a small mirror shows a face of greater size. A real explanatory gap remains: how the tiny internal image suffices for our perception of a large object and of its distance remains obscure, even if impressions and the visual spirit in the nerves are granted.

The rival **ray theory** (*shuʿāʿ*) says a ray issues from the eye in a cone with its apex at the eye and base on the visible object. There are variants: a solid cone, a cone formed by lines joining at the apex and diverging toward the base, a straight outgoing ray moving laterally across the object, or the visual ray transforming the intervening air so that the air and ray jointly become the instrument of perception. Another account rejects both ray and impression: when an illuminated object confronts the polished visual organ, with conditions present and obstacles absent, the soul receives immediate illuminative, presentational knowledge of the visible thing. The position stated as true by the commentator is that perception is produced **solely through God's creating it** on opening the eyes.

The two historically most famous positions are impression and ray. Advocates of impression argue, first, that every polished luminous body confronted by a dense coloured object receives its reflection, as a mirror does; the eye is such a polished luminous body. They cite the light apparently seen when one rubs the eye after awakening, similar reports concerning stroking a black cat in darkness, seeing a bright circle near one's nose, and the temporary perception of nearby objects upon awakening. They also cite dilation of the pupil in one eye when the other is closed and the hollow character of the visual nerves as indications of a luminous visual substance. Even if these considerations succeeded, they would establish at most the formation of a likeness, **not** that this likeness is the actual cause of seeing. Second, they analogize vision to other senses, said to receive sensible forms rather than send an agent toward the object; this is rejected as a mere analogy lacking a common explanatory ground. Third, the afterimage of the sun after looking at it for a long time is invoked, but might persist in the imagination rather than the eye, as the image can remain with closed eyes. Fourth, an object appears larger when near and smaller when distant; the theory explains this through a cone of transparent air whose apex touches the pupil and whose base lies on the surface of the visible thing, making the perceived size vary with the subtended angle. [The geometry and objections continue.]

The intermediate air is the undulating air conveying a sound whether it arises from striking (qarʿ) or separation (qalʿ). It is intermediate between the movement produced by the striking or separating bodies and the auditory cavity. The Shifāʾ describes the hearing faculty as situated in nerves spread over the inner surface of the ear, receiving the form conveyed by air violently compressed between a striker and a resisting struck body; its undulation reaches the stationary air enclosed in the auditory passage and sets it into motion. The difficulty in that wording is that it seems to mention only impact, though the author elsewhere explicitly allows separation as a source of sound.

Two objections are considered. First, how does undulating air preserve the determinate articulations and shapes of letters while entering narrow channels and striking solid walls? Second, if sound inheres in the entire mass of disturbed air, it should reach only one ear as a whole and only one listener hear it. If sound inheres in each constituent portion, each hearer should hear it repeatedly, as many times as portions of air reach the ear. The reply to these objections is introduced by an expression of possibility rather than an unqualified demonstration. If audible sound and its perception depend on air, the mere contact of celestial spheres could neither produce sound nor transmit it to us through an impenetrable celestial body. Yet ancient authorities are said to have attributed extraordinary sounds and harmonies to the heavens. Pythagoras is reported to have ascended in soul to the higher realm, heard the notes of the spheres through the purity of his soul, and subsequently arranged musical intervals and developed the art of music on returning to bodily faculties. The commentator reports rather than independently establishes this account.

Vision. On the anatomical scheme received by the commentators, seven pairs of nerves issue from the brain. The first pair begins deep within the anterior ventricles near two protrusions resembling nipples. These small hollow nerves pass across and intersect, so the nerve coming from the right passes to the left side and the one from the left to the right, reaching the respective pupils. That the perceptive powers inhabit these locations is argued from damage to them impairing the associated acts of perception.

Several accounts of sight are debated. The impression theory (inṭibāʿ) says that an image or likeness (shabaḥ) of the visible object is formed in the crystalline moisture of the eye, comparable to a mirror. When a coloured illuminated object confronts the receptive surface through a transparent medium, its image arises there, not because some portion of the object detaches and travels to the eye, but in the way a reflection occurs in a mirror. Replies are that seeing by an image need not make the image the object seen—what is seen is the thing whose image is impressed, as in the earlier discussion of knowledge—and that likeness demands correspondence of shape and colour, not equality of magnitude, just as a small mirror shows a face of greater size. A real explanatory gap remains: how the tiny internal image suffices for our perception of a large object and of its distance remains obscure, even if impressions and the visual spirit in the nerves are granted.

The rival ray theory (shuʿāʿ) says a ray issues from the eye in a cone with its apex at the eye and base on the visible object. There are variants: a solid cone, a cone formed by lines joining at the apex and diverging toward the base, a straight outgoing ray moving laterally across the object, or the visual ray transforming the intervening air so that the air and ray jointly become the instrument of perception. Another account rejects both ray and impression: when an illuminated object confronts the polished visual organ, with conditions present and obstacles absent, the soul receives immediate illuminative, presentational knowledge of the visible thing. They also cite dilation of the pupil in one eye when the other is closed and the hollow character of the visual nerves as indications of a luminous visual substance. Even if these considerations succeeded, they would establish at most the formation of a likeness, not that this likeness is the actual cause of seeing. Second, they analogize vision to other senses, said to receive sensible forms rather than send an agent toward the object; this is rejected as a mere analogy lacking a common explanatory ground. Third, the afterimage of the sun after looking at it for a long time is invoked, but might persist in the imagination rather than the eye, as the image can remain with closed eyes. Fourth, an object appears larger when near and smaller when distant; the theory explains this through a cone of transparent air whose apex touches the pupil and whose base lies on the surface of the visible thing, making the perceived size vary with the subtended angle. title: Refutation of emitted rays, geometrical optics, and the common sense (vol. II, pp. 19–21)
en:
The geometrical argument from apparent magnitude says that as an object approaches the eye the sides of the visual cone shorten and its angle increases; as it recedes, the reverse occurs. The image contained within the larger angle is consequently larger than one in a smaller angle. This works, the defenders of impression say, only when perception is located at the apex, as in their theory, not at the base of the cone, as in a simple version of emitted-ray theory, since the object's base need not vary. The objection is that the inference has not eliminated all other explanations, including explanations proposed by ray-theorists themselves; and whether increasing the angle necessarily enlarges the *apparent object* requires examination. These are among the reasons why the inference is called weak.

Supporters of the **emitted-ray** account advance four arguments. (1) Where a person's visual ray is scant, nearby things are more clearly seen because the ray becomes dispersed at a distance; where it is abundant and thick, distant things may be seen better because the passage through a long interval makes it finer and more transparent. An impression-only account, they claim, does not explain such variation. (2) Those who see in darkness rather than daylight are said to have too little visual ray, which is dispersed by sunlight but gathered and strengthened at night, whereas those who see better by day have a ray too thick until sunlight refines it. (3) When one reads a sheet of writing, the line directly attended to is distinct while the rest is unclear because the axis of the visual cone apprehends more distinctly than its margins. (4) In darkness one may perceive light apparently proceeding from one's eye toward the nose, or when closing the eyes before a lamp, rays seeming to connect the eye and lamp.

The answer is that these phenomena at most suggest some luminous material or process in the eye; they do not prove that vision occurs *by bodily rays exiting it*. The commentator allows that traditional physiology posits a luminous “visual spirit” (*rūḥ bāṣira*) in the organ of sight and describes an imaginary cone between the eye and visible object, with its apex at the crystalline humour. That spirit may vary in strength with distance, become excessively rarefied or dense, and need different conditions to receive a distinct image. A visible light may even be produced in receptive bodies confronting the eye, especially along the visual axis. Avicenna suggests that the ray-theorists may have been using the expression figuratively for something of this kind.

Taken literally, the outgoing-ray theory is rejected. If a ray is an accident or quality, its physical travel in the alleged manner is clearly untenable. If it is a luminous body, how could bodily matter pour from a small eye in an instant, extend across half the sphere of the world, then return as the eyelid shuts or vanish and be replaced whenever it opens? How could it move in every direction without compulsion or will, penetrate and perforate the heavens to perceive stars, remain unaffected by wind, and reach only what stands opposite the eye when waves of sound are deflected by winds? Nor do we see the moon before the fixed stars after a travel-time difference proportional to their supposed distances: distant celestial bodies are visually presented together. If rays physically pass through gaps, we ought to see through porous earthenware, since its pores are proved by seepage, rather than through glass and water; and visibility through pores should reveal fragmented portions proportional to their openings, not a single whole object. Analogous objections apply if visual rays are said to modify the intervening air into a connected organ of sight.

**The science of perspective and mirrors** (*ʿilm al-manāẓir wa-l-marāyā*) is treated as a special discipline. Its practitioners often formulate the geometry as if a ray issued from the eye toward the object—as though light from sun, moon or another luminous body formed a cone with its apex at the source and base at what it faced. More distant objects subtend a narrower angle and thus appear smaller, until they become imperceptible. Objects in water appear larger than in air because some visual paths proceed directly and others are bent at the surface. When an object is close to the surface these paths are not distinguished and it is seen as enlarged; with greater separation, different paths can produce distinct images. If one eye is pressed or displaced while looking at the moon, double vision occurs, since the paths of the two eyes are no longer made to coincide in the common sense at one position. Similar doubling occurs when the fingers act on the eye while viewing a lamp. Looking at the water under the moon, one may see the moon reflected in the water as well as in the sky. A polished mirror returns the path from the eye toward an object situated in the appropriate relation to the reflecting surface. Trees beside a river appear inverted: the ray reflected toward the tree's top takes a path from a place closer to the observer than the path toward its base, and because the soul habitually interprets sight as a straight path, it projects these reflecting paths through the surface and apparently places the top lower in the water. The precise geometry belongs in the specialist science. These constructions explain appearances but do not establish the literal emission of a physical ray.

**Are conditions for vision necessary and sufficient?** Philosophers, followed by Muʿtazilites, claim that vision cannot occur without its specified prerequisites and must occur whenever all are present. For necessity they cite ordinary experience: when one condition is missing vision fails. But actual absence does not prove impossibility. For sufficiency they argue that if all the conditions could occur without vision, towering mountains or beautiful gardens might stand directly in front of us without our seeing them; this consequence is claimed to be plainly false. The reply distinguishes two senses. If it means such a failure is *intrinsically possible*, its impossibility is not conceded; if it means ordinary reason could lack firm certainty that such objects are absent, the entailment is denied, for such certainty belongs to customary knowledge, as previously discussed. Some philosophers limit the alleged requirements to the soul's present form of connection with the body or to the visual faculty's present strength, not to every conceivable mode of perception, such as the vision promised in the next life. A reflected face is regarded as “equivalent to confronting” the viewer, rather than directly confronted.

**Internal senses.** Five internal powers are inferred from observable phenomena, though additional ones cannot be ruled out a priori. A schematic classification distinguishes apprehending powers from powers assisting apprehension: apprehension of *forms* or *intentions*; retention of forms or intentions; and the power manipulating such contents. The **common sense** (*al-ḥiss al-mushtarak*, Greek *phantasia* as transmitted here), also called the tablet of the soul, is the faculty in which the sensible forms delivered by the external senses are assembled.

Three arguments are offered for it. **First**, we judge across different senses that *this yellow thing* is *this hot thing*, or this sweet or fragrant thing. Since sight alone apprehends colours, touch tactile qualities and so forth, none of the five outward senses by itself contains both sides of the judgement; an inner faculty must unite them. **Second**, sleepers and persons in delirium see particular scenes which are neither present externally nor present in an outward sense, so some internal power must be the seat of these appearances. **Third**, a falling drop swiftly moving appears as a straight line, and a rapidly revolving flame as a circle. No single position of the object can produce that extended image in the eye, which is directed only toward what is then opposite it; hence impressions must persist for a short period in another faculty and join the impressions of successive positions. To deny this distinction, the commentator considers obstinate.

A further objection points out that, even if the image is not stored in the visual organ, it does not follow that it must be stored in another **bodily** faculty: it might be present directly in the soul. The sleeping images and the forms compared across the senses might likewise be present there. We can judge that “this yellow” is a colour and “Zayd” is a human being. The soul certainly apprehends the universal terms in these judgements; if both terms must be present to what judges, why may the particular not also be represented in the soul? The Peripatetic argument for a separate common sense therefore depends on the disputed premise that sensible particulars are not imprinted directly in the soul. [The reply continues in the next passage.]

title: Imagination, estimation, memory, cogitation, and animal movement (vol. II, pp. 22–25)
en:
The defenders of a separate **common sense** reply to the preceding objection that the soul indeed apprehends both universals and particulars and judges between them, but that the particular forms do not inhere in it; rather, as will be argued, they are impressed in its bodily instruments. A judgement comparing two sensible particulars therefore requires a shared instrument. The commentator again finds this inconclusive. The soul might have the compared representations before it even though they are imprinted in *different* instruments, just as the soul judges a universal represented in itself against a particular represented in an organ. This would show that the five external senses are insufficient for judgement both in the presence and absence of the object and may perhaps require an inward correlate for each, but would not yet establish a single distinct common sense. Al-Rāzī also objects that tasting and touching certainly do not occur in the brain itself, nor merely in the conducting nerve. The answer concedes that the brain is not the sole or specifically dedicated instrument for taste and touch, but denies that it has no role at all: damage in the brain can impair these senses. Thus tasting begins in the tongue and is completed through the nerve leading to it from the brain, and analogously for other senses, culminating in the common sense. This remains a theory, not a conclusive division of faculties.

**The imaginative store (*al-khayāl*).** Two arguments seek to establish its existence and difference from the common sense. First, sensory images are both *received* and *retained* in us. Reception and preservation are different acts, so—according to the rule that one single power produces only one primary effect—there must be distinct principles. The common sense receives; imagination preserves. Retention is needed for the ordering of life: without recognising a thing previously seen on seeing it again, animals could not reliably distinguish what is beneficial from what harms. Several objections follow. Retention presupposes reception; why may the same power not do both? The common sense already apprehends several sensory kinds, and the rational soul both receives intelligible forms and directs the body. These are counterexamples to an unrestricted one-power/one-act principle. It is replied that the material substrate may account for reception while an imaginative power accounts for preservation, as earth receives a shape through its matter and retains it through its form or quality, dryness. The common sense's several acts arise from different external routes, and the soul's acts from its diverse instruments. But these very replies undermine the argument for two *essentially distinct* powers: a single power could receive and preserve under differing conditions. A different reply—that receiving and apprehending are passions rather than actions, so do not multiply a source's *active* effects—is likewise not enough to establish two powers.

Second, the distinction between **forgetting** and **inattention** is invoked. Some images disappear entirely from the common sense and require a new sensation: this is forgetting. Others depart from awareness but return immediately when attention is turned to them: this is inattention. Were the images not stored in another faculty from which the common sense could retrieve them, the distinction would vanish. It is objected that the common sense itself could retain them while attention alone determines whether the soul notices them. The answer is that this would collapse actual sensation into imagination, for both would be a sensory image present in the common sense with attention, whereas imagining a previously seen object is not seeing it, nor imagining a taste tasting it. Perception comes from the external senses; imagining from the inner store. But the difference might depend instead on whether the object is currently present to the external senses, or on the varying strength of impression, without two essentially different faculties of reception and storage.

Al-Rāzī attempts to refute the bodily imagination by considering someone who has travelled widely and seen innumerable cities and persons. If all their images were received in a single portion of the cerebral spirit, they would be confused; if each image required a separate region, something enormous would be represented in a minute part. The reply is that this mistakes images for material bodies. Multiple distinct representations may be successively present in one receptive subject, and a representation of a very large object may be present in a very small one; the physical constraints on the inherence of an accident or the occupancy of a body in a place cannot simply be transferred to representational content.

**Estimation (*al-wahm*).** This apprehends *particular intentions* or nonsensory meanings (*maʿānī juzʾiyya*) found in sensible things—for example, the particular hostility associated with Zayd or what a sheep apprehends in a wolf. The qualification “particular” distinguishes it from the rational soul's apprehension of hostility in general. “Intentions” here simply contrasts with sensible *forms*: a meaning not directly apprehended by sight, hearing or the other external senses, rather than a meaning that must be further qualified as nonsensible. Its apprehension shows that some power receives such meanings; their not being transmitted by the external senses distinguishes estimation from the common sense; and their particularity, on the philosophers' assumption that the rational soul does not immediately apprehend particulars as such, distinguishes it from rational intellect. This argument must still meet the question: if one faculty can receive several types of sensible form, why may it not also receive their associated particular intentions?

Some would show that estimation receives both forms and intentions because, seeing something yellow, we judge it to be honey and sweet, or because what apprehends a particular person's hostility must apprehend the person himself. But the commentator finds the inference weak. The true judge may be the soul, to which the image and intention are separately presented through different instruments; they need not inhabit a single internal faculty. A difficulty remains when such judgements are made by non-rational animals, for which the disputed theory does not establish a rational soul performing the judgement.

**The preservative or memory faculty (*al-ḥāfiẓa*).** It preserves estimated intentions as the imagination preserves sensible forms. Its distinctness is inferred from the difference between receipt and preservation, and from the difference between storing intentions and storing images. Some call it the *remembering* faculty (*dhākira*) because through it we attend to a stored item after inattention; others call it *recollective* (*mutadhakkira*) because through it one searches methodically to recover something whose representation had receded. The distinctions are unsettled.

**The composing faculty (*al-mutaṣarrifa*).** It combines and separates forms drawn from the senses and intentions apprehended by estimation: one can imagine a human with two heads or none, or a foe as a friend and conversely. This activity continues in sleep and wakefulness. In dialectical discovery it can search what is stored in memory and obtain a middle term; it imitates sensible presentations and temperamental states and moves to opposites and similarities. Its spontaneous activity need not be ordered. The rational soul can, however, employ it deliberately. When it is used by the faculty of estimation without intellectual government it is called *imaginative composition* (*mutakhayyila*); when employed by intellect alone or together with estimation it is *cogitative* (*mufakkira*).

**Locations assigned to the five inner faculties.** Traditional anatomy distinguishes three cerebral cavities, the first largest and the middle smallest, forming a passage from the front to the rear. Injury to the front of the first ventricle is used to locate the common sense there; analogous lesions place the image-store toward the rear of the first cavity, imagination/composition in the middle cavity, estimation toward the front of the final cavity, and memory toward the rear. The multiplication of faculties itself depends on the difference of their activities together with the one-power/one-effect principle. One can object that this principle, if sound, applies only to what is one in every respect. Why not posit the rational soul—or a single faculty operating through different instruments—as the common apprehender? The account that the rational soul apprehends and bodily powers serve it as instruments is admitted by many investigators, although it is difficult to apply to the sensory judgements of non-rational animals. A single *bodily* power using several distant organs as instruments is also problematic: how could a corporeal faculty be situated in one organ yet act through another in which it does not inhere? The commentator acknowledges the difficulty of demonstrating the premises used both to multiply the powers and to establish their specific locations.

A purposive explanation of their arrangement is also proposed: the common sense is located at the front to receive easily from the outer senses; the store of forms lies just behind it; estimation should be near the image store so particular meanings and forms may be coordinated; the store of intentions behind estimation; and the composing faculty in the middle, able to take easily from both kinds of content. Avicenna himself hesitates. In the *Shifāʾ* he suggests that the estimating, recollecting, imagining, cogitating and judging powers may be one power, judging in virtue of itself and imagining or recollecting according to its changing actions. He also hesitates whether simple retention of intentions and active recollection of what has receded are two powers or one. Physicians, concerned chiefly with preserving health and correcting dysfunction, need not determine the metaphysical divisions of the faculties. They often distinguish only a forward cerebral power called common sense/imagination, a middle power called cogitation/estimation, and a rear power called memory/recollection.

**Motive faculties.** The author treats these more briefly because theological disputes depend more directly on cognition than on the physical instruments of bodily movement. “Motive” includes both the power that produces movement and the power that impels or desires it. The latter is the *appetitive* or *impulsive* power (*shawqiyya*, *nuzūʿiyya*), divided into a concupiscible power moving toward what is believed or supposed beneficial and an irascible power moving toward what is believed or supposed harmful. The power producing bodily movement lengthens and narrows an organ, or contracts and broadens it, through the corresponding extension and contraction of muscles and nerves. The traditional anatomical account makes muscle a combination of nerves, ligaments or tendons arising near the bones, flesh occupying spaces between interlaced parts, and membranes; nerve is a white, pliant structure arising from brain or spinal cord, soft in bending but resistant to being pulled apart.

It might seem that an additional motive power originates the desire itself, as in longing for a familiar person, a captive's desire for liberty, or the soul's inclination toward a noble act. But the nearer principle of such desire is the *representation* of an object, by imagination or understanding; that principle therefore belongs to cognition. Finally, a particular sensory or motive faculty may be absent from a species, allegedly as sight in certain scorpions or imagination in moths; it may be congenitally absent from an individual, as in someone born blind or without a movement; or it may be lost through injury or disease. This closes the treatment of common vegetative and animal faculties before the separate investigations of the soul and intellect.

Second, the distinction between forgetting and inattention is invoked. Some images disappear entirely from the common sense and require a new sensation: this is forgetting. Others depart from awareness but return immediately when attention is turned to them: this is inattention. Were the images not stored in another faculty from which the common sense could retrieve them, the distinction would vanish. It is objected that the common sense itself could retain them while attention alone determines whether the soul notices them. The answer is that this would collapse actual sensation into imagination, for both would be a sensory image present in the common sense with attention, whereas imagining a previously seen object is not seeing it, nor imagining a taste tasting it. Perception comes from the external senses; imagining from the inner store. But the difference might depend instead on whether the object is currently present to the external senses, or on the varying strength of impression, without two essentially different faculties of reception and storage.

Al-Rāzī attempts to refute the bodily imagination by considering someone who has travelled widely and seen innumerable cities and persons. If all their images were received in a single portion of the cerebral spirit, they would be confused; if each image required a separate region, something enormous would be represented in a minute part. The reply is that this mistakes images for material bodies. Multiple distinct representations may be successively present in one receptive subject, and a representation of a very large object may be present in a very small one; the physical constraints on the inherence of an accident or the occupancy of a body in a place cannot simply be transferred to representational content.

Estimation (al-wahm). This apprehends particular intentions or nonsensory meanings (maʿānī juzʾiyya) found in sensible things—for example, the particular hostility associated with Zayd or what a sheep apprehends in a wolf. The qualification “particular” distinguishes it from the rational soul's apprehension of hostility in general. “Intentions” here simply contrasts with sensible forms: a meaning not directly apprehended by sight, hearing or the other external senses, rather than a meaning that must be further qualified as nonsensible. Its apprehension shows that some power receives such meanings; their not being transmitted by the external senses distinguishes estimation from the common sense; and their particularity, on the philosophers' assumption that the rational soul does not immediately apprehend particulars as such, distinguishes it from rational intellect. But the commentator finds the inference weak. A difficulty remains when such judgements are made by non-rational animals, for which the disputed theory does not establish a rational soul performing the judgement.

Its distinctness is inferred from the difference between receipt and preservation, and from the difference between storing intentions and storing images. It combines and separates forms drawn from the senses and intentions apprehended by estimation: one can imagine a human with two heads or none, or a foe as a friend and conversely. In dialectical discovery it can search what is stored in memory and obtain a middle term; it imitates sensible presentations and temperamental states and moves to opposites and similarities. Its spontaneous activity need not be ordered. The rational soul can, however, employ it deliberately. The multiplication of faculties itself depends on the difference of their activities together with the one-power/one-effect principle. One can object that this principle, if sound, applies only to what is one in every respect. Why not posit the rational soul—or a single faculty operating through different instruments—as the common apprehender? The account that the rational soul apprehends and bodily powers serve it as instruments is admitted by many investigators, although it is difficult to apply to the sensory judgements of non-rational animals. A single bodily power using several distant organs as instruments is also problematic: how could a corporeal faculty be situated in one organ yet act through another in which it does not inhere? The commentator acknowledges the difficulty of demonstrating the premises used both to multiply the powers and to establish their specific locations.

A purposive explanation of their arrangement is also proposed: the common sense is located at the front to receive easily from the outer senses; the store of forms lies just behind it; estimation should be near the image store so particular meanings and forms may be coordinated; the store of intentions behind estimation; and the composing faculty in the middle, able to take easily from both kinds of content. Physicians, concerned chiefly with preserving health and correcting dysfunction, need not determine the metaphysical divisions of the faculties. They often distinguish only a forward cerebral power called common sense/imagination, a middle power called cogitation/estimation, and a rear power called memory/recollection.

Motive faculties. The author treats these more briefly because theological disputes depend more directly on cognition than on the physical instruments of bodily movement. “Motive” includes both the power that produces movement and the power that impels or desires it. The latter is the appetitive or impulsive power (shawqiyya, nuzūʿiyya), divided into a concupiscible power moving toward what is believed or supposed beneficial and an irascible power moving toward what is believed or supposed harmful. The power producing bodily movement lengthens and narrows an organ, or contracts and broadens it, through the corresponding extension and contraction of muscles and nerves. The traditional anatomical account makes muscle a combination of nerves, ligaments or tendons arising near the bones, flesh occupying spaces between interlaced parts, and membranes; nerve is a white, pliant structure arising from brain or spinal cord, soft in bending but resistant to being pulled apart.

It might seem that an additional motive power originates the desire itself, as in longing for a familiar person, a captive's desire for liberty, or the soul's inclination toward a noble act. But the nearer principle of such desire is the representation of an object, by imagination or understanding; that principle therefore belongs to cognition. Finally, a particular sensory or motive faculty may be absent from a species, allegedly as sight in certain scorpions or imagination in moths; it may be congenitally absent from an individual, as in someone born blind or without a movement; or it may be lost through injury or disease. This closes the treatment of common vegetative and animal faculties before the separate investigations of the soul and intellect.

title: Definition of soul as first perfection; the relation of soul to body, form, and power (vol. II, pp. 25–28)
en:
**The second article concerns immaterial entities.** It consists of two chapters, the first treating soul and the second intellect. An immaterial substance that is related to a body by way of administration and governance is termed a *soul* (*nafs*); one without such a relation is an *intellect* (*ʿaql*). “Soul” is also said of non-immaterial principles: the vegetative soul, source of nutrition, growth and generation, and the animal soul, source of sensation and voluntary movement. “Terrestrial soul” can be used for these, or also for the human rational soul.

An inclusive definition is **“the first perfection of a natural, instrumental body potentially possessed of life”** (*kamāl awwal li-jism ṭabīʿī ālī dhī ḥayāh bi-l-quwwa*). A perfection (*kamāl*) completes a species either in its own constitution, which is a **first perfection**, as the form of a sword perfects the iron into a sword, or in its subsequent attributes, which are **second perfections**, such as a sword's cutting, a body's moving and a human being's knowing. One may ask: was motion not previously called a first perfection? Yes, but relative to what is in potency *as such*, for motion is the first actuality arising in it; relative to the essence of the body whose motion it is, motion counts as a second perfection.

The word “body” here names the **genus**, taken without stipulating whether it exists separately or together with an additional determination (*lā bi-sharṭ*), so that the corresponding generic nature remains incomplete until a specific difference makes it an actual kind. It does not mean body taken on condition of existing in isolation (*bi-sharṭ lā*): so considered it is a material component preceding the specific composite and not predicable of the whole; the soul is then its *form*, not its species-constituting perfection. The analysis was established in the discussion of quiddity. Body is mentioned because the definition is of the soul as a *relationally described principle*: that from which the operations of life proceed in a body. The definition is not concerned in the first instance with whether that principle, considered in itself, is substance or accident, immaterial or material; the body belongs to the definition by virtue of the relation, as a building belongs to the explanation of a builder.

“Natural” excludes manufactured composites and their artificial forms. “Instrumental” means furnished with faculties or organs such as those of nutrition and growth. Together with “first perfection,” these qualifications exclude second perfections, the perfections of separate intellects and accidents, and the forms of artificially assembled structures. “Instrumental” also excludes elemental simples and minerals, whose characteristic actions are not attributed to organs. The expression “potentially possessed of life” is not redundant. It cannot mean that the body is actually alive, nor that *all* life-functions must proceed from it, for otherwise only the human soul would satisfy the definition, not the plant and animal souls. It means that some acts characteristic of living things can arise from it, even if those acts do not all require life in the same way. Simple and mineral bodies would not be excluded merely by that possibility. The qualification is particularly meant to distinguish terrestrial soul from a **celestial soul**, on the view that there is one soul of the total heavenly sphere and its component spheres and stars function as its instruments. On that theory the heaven is instrumental; nevertheless its understanding and voluntary motion are held to be perpetual and in actuality, unlike the terrestrial powers of nutrition, growth, reproduction, sensation, voluntary motion and intellectual understanding, which can be in potency. Those who assign an individual soul to each celestial sphere and deny that the sphere is “instrumental” do not need the qualification, which is why most omit it. Abū al-Barakāt uses “potentially living” in place of “instrumental.” The ancients often defined soul simply as the first natural perfection of an instrumental body.

The wording and word-order matter. Sometimes “natural” qualifies “perfection” and precedes “body”; sometimes it qualifies “body.” It should not be taken as an awkward predicate of “perfection” while following “body” in the received phrase, nor is this solved by similarly making “instrumental” qualify “perfection.” Al-Rāzī reports the straightforward alternative “first *natural* perfection of an instrumental body.” It might be objected that, if the added qualification “potentially living” alone excludes celestial souls, the shorter definition would equally apply to earthly and heavenly souls, whereas some philosophers have said that “soul” is common to them only as a homonymous term: the former acts in diverse ways and the latter continuously in one way; no single delimitation embraces both without also including elementary forms or excluding plants. The reply is that this claim assumes the view that every sphere has a soul with no diversity of instrument or activity. Even then it is doubtful, because the *Shifāʾ* describes soul as the principle of activities not uniformly proceeding without will. That formula could extend to both terrestrial and celestial souls: the former have several kinds of activities, and the latter act voluntarily, whether through several activities on one view or a single constant voluntary activity on the better view.

Soul can also be considered a **form**, because it combines with matter to constitute a plant or animal, or a **power**, because it initiates the body's acts. Why privilege *perfection* as the defining word? The term “form” strictly names what inheres in matter and cannot embrace a separate rational soul without extension of usage or a new convention. Form is defined by its relation to *matter*; perfection by its relation to the **completed species**. When defining what completes a natural body as this species and source of its operations, the relation to the already constituted species is more relevant than the relation to the relatively distant, indeterminate material component, which is not yet the species and of which these operations are not predicated. This condenses the argument of the *Shifāʾ*. Al-Rāzī's formulation adds that reference to the species implicitly includes its material component, but the reverse is not true, and the species is nearer the generic nature than matter is. That can be understood as meaning that a vague generic nature becomes determinate through the constitutive difference, or soul; genus and species are not separately existing things, but one reality considered indeterminately or determinately. It would be a mistake to infer that the perfection is related simply to the generic nature itself and that the intervening reference to species is superfluous.

“Power” is also less suitable because it is equivocal between an active source, such as a mover, and a capacity for reception or affection, as in sensing. Both are relevant to living and intellective realities. Including one excludes some aspects of the soul; including both produces ambiguity in a definition. Moreover a soul is both a principle of activities and what completes a species; “power” conveys only the former, whereas “perfection” can convey both. Hence the matn uses a broad formula for terrestrial and celestial souls and subsequently distinguishes them. If it is objected that the celestial souls are also said to have sensation, voluntary movement and universal understanding, the *Shifāʾ* explains that “sensation” in the terrestrial definition means receptive alteration with an impressed likeness, and “understanding” concerns the modes associated with the material intellect and intellect in habitu. The alleged celestial faculties are not of this sort.

The philosophers' principles might seem to imply **several separate souls in one human being**: a rational soul for universals, an animal soul for perception and voluntary movement, a vegetative soul for nutrition and generation, and a bodily specific form completing the organism before the rational soul attaches to it. But commentators on the *Ishārāt* deny this implication. Some composites have a mineral form which preserves their conflicting elemental constituents from dissolving toward their separate natural places. Others possess a vegetative soul which preserves them and also attracts, incorporates and disposes further matter through nutrition, growth and reproduction. Others possess an animal soul which performs those acts and perception and voluntary movement as well. Human beings possess an immaterial soul which performs all previous acts and also intellectual understanding and its consequences. The stages form a hierarchy of unified principles, rather than a mere pile of independent souls.

**The theologians**, who do not accept the philosophers' proof of essentially different kinds of bodies and natural forms as the sources of bodily effects, appeal instead to revealed evidence and rational indications. Bodies and their visible and concealed organs are constantly decomposed and replaced, while the soul or personal subject appears to continue. A person with unimpaired intelligence can be unaware of the body and its organs yet never entirely unaware of the existence of the self; and the soul tends toward acts, such as ascent, resisted by the body's ordinary tendency. The schools nevertheless disagree profoundly concerning what the soul actually is. Some identify it with fire pervading the visible body, some with air, some with water, some with the four elements together with the powers of love and domination or desire and anger. [Further views continue in the next investigation.]

title: What the soul is: corporeal theories and the first proof for immateriality (vol. II, pp. 29–31)
en:
The list of historical identifications continues: the soul has been called a combination of four elements, blood, the special temperament of each person, or an indivisible part located in the heart. Many theologians take it to consist of the *original* bodily constituents which remain throughout a person's lifetime; this may have been meant by those who describe the soul as the “perceived structure” or “perceived bodily constitution,” meaning that which is of a nature to be perceived. The majority of the theologians discussed here take it instead to be a body specifically unlike the body composing the visible organs: luminous, higher, subtle, intrinsically alive, penetrating the substances of the organs and extending through them as rosewater permeates a rose or fire pervades glowing charcoal. It does not undergo the alterations and dissolution of the ordinary body; its continued presence in the organs is life, and its departure to the realm of spirits is death. Another account makes it a subtle body arising in the heart and spreading through arteries, or one arising in the brain and travelling through the nerves. The position preferred by leading investigators among philosophers and Muslim scholars is that the soul is an **immaterial substance in itself**, connected to the body by government and direction. Its immediate instrument, on this account, is what the theologians call the *cardiac spirit*, produced within the left cavity of the heart from the subtle portions of food. The soul endows this spirit with a power to circulate through the body and supply each organ with the relevant powers previously described.

Those who argue that the soul is corporeal advance several proofs. **First**, what apprehends universals is identical to what apprehends particulars, since we predicate a universal of a particular—“this heat is heat”—and the subject judging between them must conceive both. Yet the apprehender of a particular is a body, as when we feel a flame we are immediately aware that the organ touching it experiences the heat; moreover nonhuman animals apprehend particulars without the immaterial rational souls attributed to human beings. The reply denies that the *organ itself* must be the perceiving subject: the soul perceives the heat *by means of* the organ. The soul apprehends universals in itself and particulars through instruments; making the soul alone the apprehender avoids multiplying the perceiver or making perception occur twice. But a counterdifficulty persists. This reply seems to require either immaterial souls in other animals too, or fundamentally different mechanisms of sensation: in animals the organs themselves would perceive, whereas in human beings the soul would perceive by means of those organs, despite the evident similarity of their sensory experiences.

**Second**, each person knows immediately that the “I” is here or there, standing, seated, walking, motionless and otherwise possessing properties of bodies. What possesses the proper features of a body must itself be corporeal. Relatedly, the body's sensation of fire's warmth, ice's cold or honey's sweetness is exactly the sensation of the “I”; if the two were really distinct and the “I” immaterial, one quality could not be numerically the same quality of both. The reply is that *I* primarily denotes the soul, yet is often applied to the body because of their close conjunction. When standing, sitting or other bodily predicates are ascribed to “me,” it is the body that is meant. Similarly sensation may be predicated of bodily organs by those who locate it there, while another account makes the soul sense through them. This does **not** mean—as a critic had misconstrued—that the soul, being immersed in bodily affairs, forgets its own nature and falls into extreme heedlessness, so that it mistakenly attributes to itself the properties of bodies; it is an explanation of ordinary predication.

**Third**, an immaterial soul would seem equally related to every body, leaving no reason why it should be attached to one particular body; and if attachment is possible, migration between bodies should also be possible, destroying our certainty that the Zayd of today is the person of yesterday. The answer denies equal suitability: a soul is bestowed in correspondence with the distinctive disposition produced by a particular body's balanced temperament. That body is apt for that particular soul and not for another.

**Fourth**, the apparent sense of scriptural reports implies a soul surviving the ruin of the body while performing things characteristic of bodies—entering or being shown fire, fluttering around the funeral bier, residing in lamps of light or inside green birds, and the like. Yet these reports admit figurative or analogical interpretation. Indeed, supporters of immateriality invoke the very same texts as evidence of separateness from the visible body. The assertion that an immaterial soul should not be affirmed because no demonstration establishes it is weak: it depends on the unsound principle that absence of a proof is proof of absence, and could equally be turned against corporeality.

**First argument for the soul's immateriality.** The rational soul is the *receptacle of objects that cannot inhere in matter*, and whatever receives them must itself be immaterial. The soul receives them because it understands them; the argument relies on the earlier theory that understanding requires the presence or impression of a form. An incorporeal object cannot, on that theory, have its proper likeness as an inhering corporeal form. Examples are: (a) the Necessary Existent, even if His intrinsic reality cannot be completely comprehended; (b) supposed immaterial substances, whether or not they really exist externally—for we can conceive something and then judge that it exists or does not; (c) **universal concepts**, such as humanity applicable to Zayd and ʿAmr, whose sheer conception does not rule out common predication. Such a concept cannot intrinsically be tied to one magnitude, position, sensible quality, or other determination inseparable from a material thing in the world; otherwise it could not apply to instances lacking that particular determination. If being in a material subject necessarily imposes these particular determinations while being universal excludes them, a material soul could not receive the universal form.

Further examples are (d) **indivisible objects of thought**, such as existence, unity and the point. If every concept were compounded into actual infinitely many parts, contradictions would follow; and the very existence of multiplicity as an aggregate of unities indicates the apprehensibility of the indivisible. If a simple object of thought is represented by a form that cannot divide, its immediate bearer must be simple and immaterial, for a material body is divisible, and division of what is intrinsically received in a divisible subject entails division of the received form. The qualification “intrinsically” matters. A point may terminate a line, a figure belong to a surface, or a body stand in alignment with another: such attributes belong through an additional boundary, position or relation, not simply through the whole underlying magnitude. The unity of parts as one aggregate is another case. Finally (e), we can simultaneously think *incompatible* things—blackness and whiteness, or many distinct figures—without their imagined opposition preventing their presence in the intellect. We can judge that they cannot coexist in one external material place precisely because they coexist as objects of intellectual consideration. These can be displayed as four arguments: a corporeal intellect would not apprehend immaterials, universals, simples, or mutually incompatible objects.

**Critical reply.** This argument depends on many propositions that an opponent need not concede. It assumes that understanding consists in the *inherence* of the understood thing's form rather than a relation between knower and known; that any non-immaterial soul must be divisible rather than a nonextended situated atom; that the cognitional form of an immaterial thing must itself be immaterial rather than merely its corporeal representation; that a form lodged in a subject with a particular position, size or quality must make its represented object equally particular; that the representation of an indivisible object must itself be indivisible; that representations of black and white cannot coexist even though the real qualities cannot; that their coexistence cannot be achieved in different portions of one organ; and that a divisible bearer always divides any representation which inheres intrinsically in it. Some of these premises have arguments in their favour, but the inference **does not compel** an opponent who rejects the entire theory of understanding as impression. This is a major limitation on treating the proof as demonstrative.

**Second argument begins.** The soul is said to possess characteristics absent from bodily faculties. It cognizes its own essence, instruments and acts; multiple acts of understanding do not necessarily exhaust or weaken it when bodily faculties grow weak, and intellect may even increase in capacity. One can separate this into arguments from reflexive cognition and from the endurance or improvement of understanding despite declining bodily strength. The visual, auditory, estimating and imaginative faculties are said to operate only through organs; if all cognition required an intervening instrument, how could an instrument mediate between a subject and its own essence, its own instruments, or its cognitional acts? Moreover a person in advancing age may understand better than in the period of bodily growth, while his organs become weaker. [The subsequent objections and replies continue.]

The majority of the theologians discussed here take it instead to be a body specifically unlike the body composing the visible organs: luminous, higher, subtle, intrinsically alive, penetrating the substances of the organs and extending through them as rosewater permeates a rose or fire pervades glowing charcoal. It does not undergo the alterations and dissolution of the ordinary body; its continued presence in the organs is life, and its departure to the realm of spirits is death. Another account makes it a subtle body arising in the heart and spreading through arteries, or one arising in the brain and travelling through the nerves. The position preferred by leading investigators among philosophers and Muslim scholars is that the soul is an immaterial substance in itself, connected to the body by government and direction. Its immediate instrument, on this account, is what the theologians call the cardiac spirit, produced within the left cavity of the heart from the subtle portions of food. The soul endows this spirit with a power to circulate through the body and supply each organ with the relevant powers previously described.

Those who argue that the soul is corporeal advance several proofs. First, what apprehends universals is identical to what apprehends particulars, since we predicate a universal of a particular—“this heat is heat”—and the subject judging between them must conceive both. Yet the apprehender of a particular is a body, as when we feel a flame we are immediately aware that the organ touching it experiences the heat; moreover nonhuman animals apprehend particulars without the immaterial rational souls attributed to human beings. The reply denies that the organ itself must be the perceiving subject: the soul perceives the heat by means of the organ. The soul apprehends universals in itself and particulars through instruments; making the soul alone the apprehender avoids multiplying the perceiver or making perception occur twice. But a counterdifficulty persists. This reply seems to require either immaterial souls in other animals too, or fundamentally different mechanisms of sensation: in animals the organs themselves would perceive, whereas in human beings the soul would perceive by means of those organs, despite the evident similarity of their sensory experiences.

Second, each person knows immediately that the “I” is here or there, standing, seated, walking, motionless and otherwise possessing properties of bodies. What possesses the proper features of a body must itself be corporeal. Relatedly, the body's sensation of fire's warmth, ice's cold or honey's sweetness is exactly the sensation of the “I”; if the two were really distinct and the “I” immaterial, one quality could not be numerically the same quality of both. The reply is that I primarily denotes the soul, yet is often applied to the body because of their close conjunction. When standing, sitting or other bodily predicates are ascribed to “me,” it is the body that is meant. Similarly sensation may be predicated of bodily organs by those who locate it there, while another account makes the soul sense through them. This does not mean—as a critic had misconstrued—that the soul, being immersed in bodily affairs, forgets its own nature and falls into extreme heedlessness, so that it mistakenly attributes to itself the properties of bodies; it is an explanation of ordinary predication.

Third, an immaterial soul would seem equally related to every body, leaving no reason why it should be attached to one particular body; and if attachment is possible, migration between bodies should also be possible, destroying our certainty that the Zayd of today is the person of yesterday. The answer denies equal suitability: a soul is bestowed in correspondence with the distinctive disposition produced by a particular body's balanced temperament. That body is apt for that particular soul and not for another.

Fourth, the apparent sense of scriptural reports implies a soul surviving the ruin of the body while performing things characteristic of bodies—entering or being shown fire, fluttering around the funeral bier, residing in lamps of light or inside green birds, and the like. Yet these reports admit figurative or analogical interpretation. Indeed, supporters of immateriality invoke the very same texts as evidence of separateness from the visible body. The assertion that an immaterial soul should not be affirmed because no demonstration establishes it is weak: it depends on the unsound principle that absence of a proof is proof of absence, and could equally be turned against corporeality.

First argument for the soul's immateriality. The rational soul is the receptacle of objects that cannot inhere in matter, and whatever receives them must itself be immaterial. The soul receives them because it understands them; the argument relies on the earlier theory that understanding requires the presence or impression of a form. An incorporeal object cannot, on that theory, have its proper likeness as an inhering corporeal form. Examples are: (a) the Necessary Existent, even if His intrinsic reality cannot be completely comprehended; (b) supposed immaterial substances, whether or not they really exist externally—for we can conceive something and then judge that it exists or does not; (c) universal concepts, such as humanity applicable to Zayd and ʿAmr, whose sheer conception does not rule out common predication. Such a concept cannot intrinsically be tied to one magnitude, position, sensible quality, or other determination inseparable from a material thing in the world; otherwise it could not apply to instances lacking that particular determination. If being in a material subject necessarily imposes these particular determinations while being universal excludes them, a material soul could not receive the universal form.

Further examples are (d) indivisible objects of thought, such as existence, unity and the point. If every concept were compounded into actual infinitely many parts, contradictions would follow; and the very existence of multiplicity as an aggregate of unities indicates the apprehensibility of the indivisible. If a simple object of thought is represented by a form that cannot divide, its immediate bearer must be simple and immaterial, for a material body is divisible, and division of what is intrinsically received in a divisible subject entails division of the received form. The qualification “intrinsically” matters. A point may terminate a line, a figure belong to a surface, or a body stand in alignment with another: such attributes belong through an additional boundary, position or relation, not simply through the whole underlying magnitude. The unity of parts as one aggregate is another case. Finally (e), we can simultaneously think incompatible things—blackness and whiteness, or many distinct figures—without their imagined opposition preventing their presence in the intellect. We can judge that they cannot coexist in one external material place precisely because they coexist as objects of intellectual consideration. These can be displayed as four arguments: a corporeal intellect would not apprehend immaterials, universals, simples, or mutually incompatible objects.

It assumes that understanding consists in the inherence of the understood thing's form rather than a relation between knower and known; that any non-immaterial soul must be divisible rather than a nonextended situated atom; that the cognitional form of an immaterial thing must itself be immaterial rather than merely its corporeal representation; that a form lodged in a subject with a particular position, size or quality must make its represented object equally particular; that the representation of an indivisible object must itself be indivisible; that representations of black and white cannot coexist even though the real qualities cannot; that their coexistence cannot be achieved in different portions of one organ; and that a divisible bearer always divides any representation which inheres intrinsically in it. Some of these premises have arguments in their favour, but the inference does not compel an opponent who rejects the entire theory of understanding as impression. This is a major limitation on treating the proof as demonstrative.

Second argument begins. The soul is said to possess characteristics absent from bodily faculties. It cognizes its own essence, instruments and acts; multiple acts of understanding do not necessarily exhaust or weaken it when bodily faculties grow weak, and intellect may even increase in capacity. One can separate this into arguments from reflexive cognition and from the endurance or improvement of understanding despite declining bodily strength. The visual, auditory, estimating and imaginative faculties are said to operate only through organs; if all cognition required an intervening instrument, how could an instrument mediate between a subject and its own essence, its own instruments, or its cognitional acts? Moreover a person in advancing age may understand better than in the period of bodily growth, while his organs become weaker. [The subsequent objections and replies continue.]

title: Further arguments for immateriality and celestial souls (vol. II, pp. 32–34)
en:
Further illustrations support the argument from the soul's strength despite the weakness of bodily instruments. Long experience and exercise in reasoning can improve the capacity to recall objects and derive knowledge even when the brain has become weakened by constant activity and movement. Rigorous bodily disciplines can also diminish bodily energies without correspondingly diminishing intellect. If intellectual power depended on the same bodily organs, it should decline whenever they do. **Third**, it is claimed that were the soul material, continual acts and motions would exhaust it, as they exhaust bodily capacities. The latter act only through the alteration of their subjects: senses undergo impressions from the sensed, and motive powers move organs, and such passivity is said to involve resistance overcome by force, which weakens the recipient.

The advocates themselves acknowledge that these three considerations are **persuasive rather than demonstrative**. A bodily faculty might conceivably apprehend itself and its own operations without an intermediary; the perfection of a corporeal intellectual power might depend on just the degree of bodily health which remains despite general decline, or on an organ preserved longer than the rest; and it might act without the same fatigue as familiar bodily powers. Those possibilities suffice to defeat strict necessity.

**Third major argument for immateriality.** If the rational soul were either a substance interpenetrating a body or an accident inhering in it, the soul's intellectual apprehension of *that very body* would either occur **permanently** or **never**. Both results contradict experience, since sometimes a person consciously thinks of his body or an organ such as the heart or brain and sometimes does not. The alleged entailment is explained by a dilemma. If the body's very presence suffices for the soul's apprehension, and the body is always present, then—given the completeness of the cause—its apprehension must be constant, as when the soul apprehends itself or intrinsic properties present to it without comparison to something else. A relational judgement, such as that it is immaterial or does not inhere in a subject, may depend on an act of comparison and therefore is not always apprehended. If, alternatively, apprehension of the body requires a newly formed *representation*, as the apprehension of external things does, then a material soul's representation of its own material host must occur within that host. At a time when the soul considers the body, two likenesses of the same body would coexist there: the continuously existing bodily form, and the newly produced mental form. The objector argues that two forms of the same species cannot differ numerically except through different subjects or individuating features, which the hypothesis has denied.

The commentator identifies the same disputed assumption: **that cognition requires an impressed form rather than a distinctive relation between cognizer and cognized**. If cognition consists in a relation, the permanent presence of the bodily form does not guarantee actual awareness; appropriate additional conditions may be needed, without producing a second representation. Even on representationalism, the two supposed forms need not be duplicates: one is an abstracted image in the soul, the other the original form within the body's matter. Even if both are called images of the same thing, numerical sameness of species does not obliterate their distinctness when they stand in different ways to the common subject. The derived image exists through the soul; the original form through the material body. More strictly, the original inheres in the body's matter while the derived likeness may inhere in the composite body. Furthermore the proposed dilemma applies only if the soul inheres in the body as an accident inheres in its subject, not if it is a corporeal substance entering among its parts.

**The souls of celestial spheres.** On their principles the philosophers assign to heavenly spheres both immaterial souls for universal understanding and bodily faculties for the imagination of particulars. The argument begins with circular motion. It cannot be *natural*, because a natural motion tends from an unsuitable state to a suitable one. If a circular path is natural, every point on it would be naturally sought as the sphere approaches and naturally fled as it departs, a contradiction. Straight natural motion differs: intermediate places are traversed not as independent ends but as routes to one final natural place. The problem is obvious for eternal circular motion. Even finite circular motion terminating at one particular point would make the simple homogeneous body's different parts naturally aim at different final places, and make nature prefer a longer path to a shorter one. Circular motion cannot be *compelled* either, for compulsion acts against an opposed natural tendency, which is absent on the hypothesis. Moreover a single compeller should give a consistent direction and rate of motion, whereas the celestial motions are said to vary. Therefore celestial motion is **voluntary** and accompanied by awareness.

Universal intellectual knowledge alone would seem inadequate for its successive particular motions: one universal presents its instances without privileging one, while merely corporeal particular images could not yield an unbroken and invariant perpetual course, given the finitude of bodily powers. Thus their explanation combines particular intentions and acts of perception, operating through corporeal faculties, with an enduring universal intention and understanding belonging to an immaterial soul. The sphere's immediate movement is attributed to the former, comparable to our animal faculties, and its rational ordering to the latter, comparable to our rational soul.

The argument is contested even granting the division between natural, compelled and voluntary motions, universal intellection's immateriality, and particular cognition's corporeality. Why must a *natural end* of circular motion be any one position at all? Nature could tend toward the *motion itself*, rather than toward each successive position as an independently intended end. Why say compulsion must be opposite to natural tendency, or that a compeller cannot yield different rates and directions? And why could successive particular movements not depend on **successive universal cognitions and intentions**, rather than a single generic intention of motion? Avicenna's *Ishārāt* supplies an answer to the last possibility: the end of positional motion is a specified position. A position already attained cannot still be sought; in unending circular motion no particular fixed position can be the ultimate end, for motion would cease upon reaching it. Thus the will may posit a *determinate universal description of position* toward which it always moves. Determinacy and universality are not opposed: a universal may itself have a definite essence distinguishing it from other universals even though it applies to many individuals.

The received Peripatetic account in the *Najāt* and *Shifāʾ* assigns to spheres **impressed corporeal souls**, analogous to our animal souls. The *Ishārāt* explicitly ascribes to them **immaterial souls**, analogous to our rational souls. Al-Rāzī therefore infers two souls for each sphere, one immaterial source of universal will and one impressed source of particular will. A later critical philosopher rejects this as a position no major philosopher ever held: one and the same body cannot be the instrument of two independent and essentially heterogeneous souls. Rather a *single immaterial soul* understands universals by itself and apprehends particulars through the heavenly body; particular volitions follow universal volition. The soul moves the body through the body's specific form, considered as a power in the function of motion, just as our soul acts through bodily faculties. The commentator judges the apparent difference largely terminological: al-Rāzī called that specific form or moving power a “soul” in the secondary sense, while his critic refused that designation.
