title: Are human souls of one species? Are they originated or eternal? (vol. II, pp. 34–36)
en:
**Second investigation: likeness and diversity of souls.** Some ancient philosophers regarded all human and animal souls as essentially alike, with differences of acts and cognition resulting from their bodily instruments. This seems obligatory for anyone who holds that souls are bodies and all bodies are essentially alike, differing only through accidents. Among those who regard human souls as immaterial, the majority likewise hold that souls agree in specific essence, but differ in qualities and stable dispositions (*malakāt*) through their temperaments and instruments. Others maintain that “soul” is a genus divided into several kinds, each kind including individuals of the same essence with related natures according to the high spiritual principle sometimes called the *complete nature* (*al-ṭibāʿ al-tāmm*) of that kind. Reports concerning human beings resembling different kinds of minerals and souls being assembled hosts—those that recognize one another coming together and those that do not separating—are interpreted as intimations of the view. Al-Rāzī in the *Maṭālib al-ʿĀliya* says that this division into several essential kinds is the view he prefers. It is not the same as claiming that **every individual soul is an entirely distinct species**, sharing no essence with any other; Abū al-Barakāt states that no one explicitly holds the latter.

The majority's proof is that the defining concept of the rational soul—such as “an immaterial substance directing a body”—is one and the same, while a definition gives the complete quiddity. The objection is that having one description does not establish unity of lowest species: a genus can be defined as one, as “animal” is defined as a sensible body moving voluntarily. Nor has it been shown that the proposed description gives the full answer to *what is it?* for each individual and every group: a further substantial difference might be required. Another argument says that human souls share the essence of “being human souls,” so if divided by specific differences they would be composites and not immaterial. But **intellectual composition into genus and differentia does not entail bodily material composition**; and the argument additionally assumes that being a soul is an essential constituent rather than an extrinsic relation.

The proponents of essential diversity argue from diversity in habits: if all souls were of one species and their differences arose exclusively from temperament, bodily state and surrounding conditions, people nearly identical in those respects should have nearly identical dispositions toward mercy and harshness, liberality and stinginess, chastity and depravity. Yet this often fails, and a person may undergo extensive bodily temperamental changes without losing his original dispositions. The commentator judges the inference **weakly persuasive**: other unobserved causes might account for those differences.

**Origination of human souls.** Whether considered material or immaterial, human souls are originated according to the theologians, because they are effects of an agent who acts by choice. The further dispute is whether the soul is created *before* the body, as a report says that God created spirits two thousand years before bodies, or after bodily development, as Qurʾānic mention of the bodily stages followed by “then We brought him forth as another creation” might suggest. The solitary report does not establish that the spirits in question are specifically human souls rather than higher substances; the verse need not mean the actual origination of the soul rather than the origination of its connection with the body.

Some philosophers defend the **pre-eternity of souls**. First, they say an originated soul cannot last forever, contrary to the agreed perpetuity of souls after death, since what comes into being after nonexistence must be liable to nonexistence. The reply distinguishes liability to subsequent annihilation—which is exactly what the argument must prove—from the general notion that a thing did not exist at some earlier time. An entity can begin to exist and continue forever through a continuously sustaining cause. Second, they argue that anything originated must be preceded by matter and time, so an originated soul would not be immaterial. Even granting the earlier claim about material preparation, the entailment fails: the originating thing may require matter as a preparatory condition or a related instrument without **inhering in it as its own subject**. Intrinsic immateriality is compatible with that.

**Aristotle and his followers** defend the soul's origination. Their first argument is that a soul existing before bodily association would be inactive and idle, whereas nature contains nothing wholly idle. The argument for its idleness depends on the later denial of transmigration. Souls separated *after* death are not idle, for they enjoy attained perfections or suffer through vices and ignorance. But the premise that nothing in nature is idle has not been proved, nor that the soul before embodiment can acquire no knowledge or perfection or have no relation to another body. Even awaiting the possibility of perfection might itself be a kind of activity.

A second argument says that each soul presupposes a body having a temperament specifically fitted to receive that soul from a universally abundant bestower; what depends on an originated condition must itself be originated. If it is objected that the soul would then perish with the bodily temperament, the reply is that the disposition may be required for its **beginning**, not its continuance, as many preparatory conditions are. But the original premise remains uncertain: the condition might be required only for the soul's *attachment*, not for the soul's own existence.

The **principal third argument** for origination is from individuality. If souls were eternal, before their attachment to bodies they would be either one or many. If one, the soul must either remain numerically one after embodiment, plainly contrary to the diversity of human beings in knowledge and ignorance, or split into many, impossible for an immaterial subject, or cease to exist and be replaced by many, which concedes origination. If eternally many, they would differ either essentially, making each its own unique kind, a thesis rejected by the opponent, or through accidents. But the philosophers maintain that distinction through accidents presupposes distinct material subjects, while bodies cannot be eternal because elementary composites are originated. Even if eternal bodies are admitted, for souls to move from such bodies into new and perishable bodies would entail **transmigration**, also rejected by the opponent.

One cannot explain eternal differentiation by each soul's awareness of its own identity, since such awareness as a *particular* content presupposes that the souls already differ. It would explain prior difference by what comes after it, a circle. If an objector says the argument equally destroys individuality after separation from bodies, when material differentiators disappear, the answer is that distinct dispositions acquired during embodiment can persist, minimally each soul's awareness of its own identity. Yet two objections remain. (1) No proof excludes each particular soul having a distinct essence, so the assumption that there must be two of the same species cannot simply be granted. (2) No independent argument has excluded an eternal body to which a soul was first attached and successive bodies thereafter. The principal anti-transmigration proof itself depends on the *origination* of souls, as will be seen; to use it to prove origination here would be circular. Recasting the argument to say that this soul's individuality could not precede *this particular body* fails if it previously had different particular bodies in an endless succession. The arguments have force as **dialectical refutations** of opponents who already concede essential sameness of souls and the impossibility of transmigration, but cannot by themselves establish those concessions.

The next enquiry considers how many souls govern a single body and whether any soul can successively govern more than one body.

title: Rejection of transmigration; post-mortem subsistence (vol. II, pp. 37–39)
en:
A rational soul and a body stand in a **one-to-one** relation. One body is not simultaneously governed by two rational souls, nor is one soul simultaneously the governor of two bodies. A further question concerns **successive** governance: might a soul leave one body and subsequently enter another (*tanāsukh*)? Three traditional objections are offered. **First**, if the soul inhabiting my present body had previously belonged to another, it ought to remember something of that body's circumstances, since knowledge, retention and remembering are said to be attributes of the same enduring substance and not to change simply because the associated body changes. This consequent is contrary to experience. **Second**, if departing souls must promptly pass into new bodies, there must be an equality between the number of bodies dying and the number beginning: otherwise some souls will be idle, several souls must occupy one body, or one soul occupy several. Yet a general catastrophe may destroy many bodies at once without their numerical replacement for many ages. **Third**, if a previously embodied soul entered a newly suitable body, two souls would be present: the arriving soul and a newly originated soul. On the philosophers' doctrine, when the ancient cause and an appropriately prepared recipient—namely the body with its suitable temperament—are complete, the new soul necessarily proceeds. If the opponent says the previous soul's attachment blocks the new one's emergence and enjoys a priority from its acquired excellence, the reply is that acquired excellence has not been shown to determine suitability for attachment. One might equally say that the creation of a new soul excludes the arrival of the old. Neither priority is established.

The commentator notes the **limits of all three arguments**. Even if their premises are granted, they chiefly exclude migration into a *new human body*. They do not yet exclude a human soul attaching to a beast, called *maskh* by certain transmigrationists, to a plant (*faskh*), to a mineral or inanimate thing (*raskh*), or to a celestial body, on one philosophical view. The premises also invite objections. The memory argument assumes that recollection does not require a particular bodily connection and cannot be obstructed by immersion in the administration of a new body or obliterated by a long interval. The numerical argument assumes that another embodiment must be necessary and immediate; if it is optional or occurs after delay, large numbers may wait, and it has not been shown that separation without such activity is impossible. Enjoyment of knowledge or suffering from ignorance might itself occupy the soul. The third argument assumes the soul begins, that its producing cause is eternally necessitating (rather than freely choosing), that a temperament alone supplies the relevant condition, and that no independent impediment remains. Each premise is disputed.

**The arguments of the transmigrationists.** Their main support is said to be weak. (1) Without another body the soul would be inactive, and nothing in existence is idle. Both propositions can be denied. (2) The soul naturally seeks completion, which it can obtain only through being attached to a body; if it could perfect itself independently it would be an *intellect* rather than a soul. Yet a thing may desire a perfection and fail to obtain it when its means or instruments have been lost, with no replacement provided. (3) Souls are said to be eternal and, unlike successive temporal events, finite in actual number; human or other bodies are infinite in succession because the celestial revolutions and their positions are without beginning. A finite set of souls could not be distributed across infinitely many successive bodies unless each soul entered more than one. The reply denies the souls' pre-eternity, denies that an actually infinite collection of eternal immaterial entities has been refuted by proofs concerning spatially ordered magnitudes, and denies the necessary infinity of bodies or their productive causes. It is also unproved that every merely conceivable body must have a soul; if the argument is confined to actually human bodies the premise that their historical series is infinite must be defended.

It is not merely a change in the outward shape of a continuous living organism, nor the recombination of the original bodily constituents and the restoration of soul at the resurrection, nor the revival of an individual through a miracle such as that given to Jesus. These are categorically different situations.

Accounts of limited transmigration are reported from philosophers but are unsupported, in the commentator's judgement, by serious evidence. The more extreme theories are rejected as contradicting decisive scriptural affirmations of bodily resurrection, the final gathering of bodies, Paradise and Hell as abodes of reward and punishment, and real bodily pleasures and pains. The theologians' affirmative evidence is the Qurʾān, transmitted reports, and the consensus of the community, which the author regards as abundant and clear. The philosophers argue for the *impossibility* of the soul's annihilation in two ways. First, its cause is eternal. If caused by it unconditionally the soul would be beginningless and endless; if its existence requires a new bodily preparedness, it can begin yet remain forever because the preparation is required only for origination, not for persistence. What receives a change survives to become characterised by the resulting state; but the very subject which actually persists cannot remain as subject of its own absolute annihilation. Since a simple soul has no persisting material substrate separable from itself, it cannot combine actual persistence with an inherent potency for its own corruption. Forms and accidents can perish because their matter or substantial bearer continues and receives their replacement; a completely immaterial subject cannot perish in that way. An objection says that the “potency for annihilation” is merely the conceptual *possibility* of nonexistence and need not inhere in a real substrate. The philosophers' answer to this objection follows in the next section.

title: Disembodied perception, the unity of the perceptive subject, and intellectual grades (vol. II, pp. 40–42)
en:
The reply to the previous proof for the impossibility of annihilation insists that the possibility at issue is a **real dispositional potentiality**, which can coexist with a thing's present existence, rather than the merely notional possibility of its nonexistence. The criticism is that a capacity to receive an *absence* does not obviously require a persisting subject which coexists with the resulting absence. Even if such a subject is required, the philosophers previously admitted that an originated immaterial soul depends upon a material preparation to which it is related without inhering in it. Why could an analogous material condition not ground its possible corruption? One answer distinguishes the intelligible preparation of an embryo's body to receive a soul governing it, given a particular temperament, from the alleged preparation of that body, by losing its temperament, to destroy the governor itself. Loss of the bodily temperament intelligibly destroys the **relation** between soul and body; it does not follow that it destroys the soul's existence.

**Fourth investigation: what knows particulars?** All agree that the human soul is what apprehends universals. But does it, as such, also apprehend particulars *in their particularity*? The theologians answer yes; the philosophers commonly attribute that to particular sense powers. Three arguments favour the unity of the perceiving subject. First, each individual judges that *this particular person* is an instance of the universal human, that this horse is not that human, that this colour differs from that taste, or that an imagined image is of a particular perceived Zayd. The judge must apprehend both things compared. Therefore a single human subject is present throughout acts of universal and particular cognition. Second, the soul administers its own particular body and directs its individual acts. Such a government requires awareness of the particulars to be governed, since universal rules alone relate indifferently to all individual cases. We plainly aim to govern *this* body, not humanity in general. Third, everyone is immediately aware of being numerically **one subject** who hears, sees and understands, though some operations require instruments. That numerically one subject indicated by “I” is the soul.

Opponents reply: (1) vision certainly belongs to the visual organ and hearing to the auditory organ, which are different powers, but this largely asserts the question as self-evident; (2) damage to those organs destroys or impairs the corresponding senses but not unrelated senses, which would be inexplicable if the soul alone were the perceiver; (3) if the soul perceived what is seen, visible objects need not be present to the eye, since the soul's own reality is unaffected by the object's nearness or absence; (4) if imagination belonged directly to a separate soul, it could not imagine situated or extended things, whose forms cannot be imprinted in what is immaterial; (5) consider two exactly similar squares adjoining another square, one on its right and the other on its left, conceived without any external model. They differ not by colour, size, figure or other specified intrinsic quality but solely by *position*. The external position is excluded by the thought experiment; a bodily subject of imagination seems required to locate the right- and left-hand images differently, whereas an immaterial subject would supply no positional individuation.

The dispute is reduced if bodily faculties are considered **instruments of cognition** and the *soul* the one true perceiver, as later philosophers explicitly maintain. That answers many objections from injury and sensory differences, but further problems remain. One: other animals cognize sensible objects without the immaterial rational souls usually reserved for human beings. It is logically possible to attribute their sensation directly to corporeal faculties and human sensation to the soul using such faculties; identity of the observed *effects* does not compel identity of the underlying *causes*. Two: if apprehension of particulars requires instruments, how does the soul directly apprehend its *own individual identity*? The reply distinguishes particulars which require an impressed form—in those the instrument is needed—from direct self-awareness which needs no representation and hence no intermediary. Three: a soul must direct itself toward *this particular body* when its connection first forms; that appears to require perception of a particular before use of the organs. The response is that the body's suitability attracts the soul through a natural, not freely chosen, inclination; such attachment need not begin in a deliberate representation. Four: the soul must apprehend the particular organs it proposes to use. It may regard them through a relation—“the instruments of this soul within this sensible body”—which picks them out without representing each in its individuality; or it may imagine them, since imaginative representations need not always arrive through current external sensation.

Yet a **fundamental difficulty** remains. The soul is said to apprehend the particular *by the image's being in an instrument*, not by its being in the soul. Either the form also becomes present in the soul, in which case the forbidden impression of a particular extended image in an immaterial subject returns; or it remains in the bodily organ alone. But then we need an account of **what change or determination in the soul constitutes knowing** rather than mere existence of an object and its likeness in an organ. If knowing is a particular *relation* between soul and object, why could the same relational theory not explain intellectual knowledge of universals without forms inhering in the soul? In short, once perception without an impressed likeness *in the perceiver* is conceded, it becomes unclear why impression must be required for universal intellection, especially when both sensory and intellectual apprehension are described as fundamentally one meaning of cognition differentiated by its objects or instruments.

**After separation from the body.** On the Peripatetic account, particular perception requires forms impressed in bodily instruments. When those instruments perish at death, the separated soul cannot apprehend particulars in that way. The theologians deny that such instruments are necessary: either cognition is not an impressed form in the soul or senses at all, or a particular form can itself be cognized by the separated soul. The commentator further reports as consonant with Islamic principles that separated souls may have new particular cognitions and knowledge of certain events among the living, especially persons with whom they were connected in the world. This grounds the traditional account of visiting graves and seeking the assistance of pious departed souls in receiving benefits and warding off troubles: the soul is said to retain some relation to its body and burial-place, so a living visitor directed toward the departed soul may enter into an encounter or exchange of influences. This is a *reported doctrinal explanation*, not a claim that a proposed psychological mechanism has been empirically verified.

**Fifth investigation: the theoretical and practical intellects.** “Power” can mean both a source of acting and changing something else and a capacity for being affected and changed. The soul considered in its *receptive* perfection through knowledge from higher principles is called the **theoretical intellect** (*ʿaql naẓarī*); considered in its direction of the body so as to perfect its substance and operations it is the **practical intellect** (*ʿaql ʿamalī*). Bodily governance also ultimately contributes to the soul's perfection because the body is an instrument of knowledge and practice. The commonly enumerated degrees of theoretical intellect are four: complete actuality, and dispositions toward that completion that are strong, intermediate or weak.

The weakest disposition is mere potentiality for cognition, the **material intellect** (*ʿaql hayūlānī*), analogous to first matter lacking determinate forms while capable of receiving them, and to a child's mere capacity to learn writing. The intermediate disposition is the **intellect in habitu** (*ʿaql bi-l-malaka*), able to acquire conclusions once primary necessities are possessed, as someone who has already gained the underlying skills for learning to write. Individuals differ greatly in this readiness according to their capabilities and dispositions. The further degrees follow.

title: Degrees of intellect, practical wisdom, the sciences, and virtues (vol. II, pp. 43–45)
en:
The third degree of theoretical intellect is the readiness to **recall previously acquired theoretical conclusions at will without having to derive them afresh**: the knowledge has been stored and returns through attention, like the trained writer who can write at any time although not presently writing. This is the **intellect in actuality** (*al-ʿaql bi-l-fiʿl*), because of its closeness to actual intellectual exercise. The fourth is the *present* contemplation of theoretical knowledge, as writing actually occurs when a writer writes. This is called the **acquired intellect** (*al-ʿaql al-mustafād*) because its actual knowledge is received from a source beyond the soul, traditionally the *Active Intellect* which actualizes our potential understanding as sunlight actualizes vision.

The philosophical terminology is unstable. Sometimes the names designate dispositions and their perfections, sometimes the soul as possessing them, and sometimes faculties in the soul that originate those dispositions. Thus the “material intellect” can mean the soul's readiness for immediate basic cognition, the pure receptive power, or the soul at its original stage of formation. The intellect in habitu can mean the possession of primary truths with the ability to proceed to conclusions. Avicenna calls it the form of the first intelligibles accompanied by the ability to acquire further ones, analogous to light preparing vision. The acquired intellect can mean the intelligible objects themselves actually present. title: Extraordinary psychic operations, dreams, waking visions, and animal understanding (vol. II, pp. 46–48)
en:
**Sixth investigation: extraordinary states and operations of souls.** The theologians hold that what occurs is created directly by God and do not credit the soul with an independent power to produce these effects. Philosophers attempt to explain some extraordinary phenomena through the soul's powers. The discussion has three parts: extraordinary **actions** associated with souls, cognitions during **sleep**, and unusual cognitions during **wakefulness**.

The first includes prophets' miracles and saints' wonders, the evil eye attributed to certain persons without their intending it, and magical operations, incantations and similar acts performed through particular practices. The philosophical explanation is that, just as higher immaterial substances are said to influence the world of generation and corruption, a soul influences the body it governs. This is not because it is physically impressed in the body, but by a special affective relation between soul and body. It might therefore have the capacity to affect **other bodies**, animals or material things, and some souls might act almost as the soul of a larger portion of the world. Affinity to certain bodies could make the influence stronger. Such thinkers regard it as possible for a powerful soul to alter air into clouds and produce rain, even an overwhelming flood, or to cause motion and rest, condensation and rarefaction, with winds, lightning, earthquakes or springs, as well as to remove illness or harm. Alternatively a noble soul may desire good and pray, acquiring a disposition which God accepts by bringing about a particular possible event. When an extraordinary event arises in association with a virtuous soul, it is classed as a **miracle** if accompanied by a claim to prophecy, otherwise as a **saintly wonder** (*karāma*).

Other purported methods are distinguished: an involuntary harmful effect associated with someone's gaze (*ʿayn*, the evil eye); practices called *siḥr*; formulae and incantations allegedly drawing on spiritual beings (*ʿazāʾim*); supplications to stars (*daʿwat al-kawākib*); configurations combining celestial and terrestrial forces (*ṭilasmāt*); operations depending on elemental peculiarities (*nīranjāt*); and geometric contrivances (*ḥiyal handasiyya*). These may be combined in devices for lifting weights, conveying water, moving figures or producing whistles, using physical properties and mathematical proportions together. They are described as traditional classifications of effects, not endorsed causal powers.

**Dreams.** According to the philosophers, the soul is normally occupied by incoming sense impressions and seldom free to turn toward immaterial spiritual substances. When the outer senses become quiescent in sleep, and the sensible spirit retreats from them, the soul may be connected with those substances and receive intelligible forms associated with its own concerns and those of family, children, property or country. The objects may be particulars or universals which the imaginative faculty represents in particular images; these pass into the inner image-store and common sense, so that they are experienced as if seen. Where the image remains close to the original perception, the dream may need no interpretation. When imagination has converted it into something analogous, opposed, or symbolically connected with its source, **dream interpretation** works backward: it reconstructs successive transformations until reaching the original representation. The imagination's tendency to imitate and substitute may take the dream farther and farther from its beginning, and where no discoverable relation connects them, the vision is classed as a confused dream (*aḍghāth aḥlām*).

A dream need not, on this theory, originate in a higher spiritual source. A residual sense image may persist in imagination and emerge during sleep; ordinary cogitation may combine images and later project them into common sense; or changes in the temperament of the bodily spirit may alter the images. On the humoral explanation, predominance of yellow bile yields yellow dreams, blood red ones, black bile dark ones, and phlegm images of ice and snow. These are the causal claims of medieval psychology.

**Waking experiences.** An especially strong soul might allegedly retain its contact with higher immaterial principles even while governing the body. If the imaginative power is also strong, it may direct the common sense away from ordinary external sensation, allowing impressions of past or future matters to be presented as voices, written words, human or angelic speakers, unseen callers, or visible figures not actually present to the outward senses. Such experiences can also arise, the philosophers admit, from defective organs in sickness or madness, strong bewilderment of the senses, intensely shimmering objects, fear and anxious imagination, or ascetic practices that weaken bodily preoccupations. These are philosophical hypotheses concerning the *apparent cause* of the experiences. The theological position expressed here is that **God is the creator** of the occurrences, whatever customary or accompanying conditions are found.

**Might other animals have immaterial rational souls?** The majority of philosophers deny that animals other than humans possess immaterial souls capable of universals. Some suspend judgement: there is no sufficient proof of such souls, but neither is their absence demonstratively certain. The quick response “if they had souls they would be human, because a human consists only of soul and body” fails, since souls might be essentially diverse or differ through specific features not yet known. Some scholars defend nonhuman rational cognition on philosophical and scriptural grounds. They cite the ordered hexagonal cells of bees, coordinated behaviour, the food-storing of ants, navigation by camels, horses and other animals in dark conditions, elephants' varied capacities and birds' and insects' ways of treating injuries—all as instances of complex purposive behaviour sometimes surpassing human skill. Scriptural texts are cited concerning birds knowing their prayer and praise, God's revelation to bees, mountains and birds responding to David, the hoopoe's report to Solomon, and the ant warning the others to enter their dwellings. The author reports these arguments while leaving their metaphysical force open to further examination.

title: Arguments for separate intellects and alleged ten celestial intellects (vol. II, pp. 48–50)
en:
**Second chapter: the separate intellect (*ʿaql*).** Philosophers argue for the existence of immaterial intellects through several lines of reasoning. **First**, the first effect proceeding from the Necessary Existent must be a substance separate in its essence and operations—what is meant by an “intellect.” It must be a *substance*, not an accident: an accident requires a bearer. If that bearer is separately produced by the First, a multitude of effects would issue immediately from what is absolutely one. If the bearer is produced by the accident itself, the accident would need to precede its own existence, since it cannot exist before its bearer. The first effect must also be *separate*. A body, compounded of matter and form, would again involve multiplicity. Matter and form cannot exist independently of one another; to make one produce the other would require matter, whose character is reception rather than production, to act as an efficient cause, or require form to act before the matter whose partnership enables its operation. Nor can the first effect be a *soul* independent in essence but dependent on a body in operation: if its body's existence comes immediately from the First, multiplicity again results; if the soul produces the body on which its productive operation depends, it must exercise the operation before its own condition exists. The conclusion is that the first thing caused must be both immediately created by the First and able to cause a second thing without such additional dependence. Only a separate intellect is said to have that character.

**Second**, the direct producer of the first body must be a separate intellect. If it were the Necessary Existent, multiple bodily constituents would proceed from absolute unity. If it were a body or an accident in a body, the first body would have to exist already as a condition of the cause. If it were a soul, its bodily organ would be either the first body, creating the same priority problem, or another body, which could not be prior unless other bodies were already produced. Matter or form cannot produce the very first body without the other constituent, and their combination is itself already a body. Therefore a self-sufficient immaterial productive source is required.

**Objections to the first two arguments.** The prohibition on more than one immediate effect from an absolutely one cause has not been established; even if the philosophers' principle were granted in one setting, why could an agent choosing freely not produce several things through acts of will? The first effect need not be confined to the listed kinds: an attribute of the Necessary could be the initial produced item, and the second and third could then issue through that attribute or through the essence considered under that aspect. Moreover, the first effect need not itself efficiently produce all later things; it might simply be an intermediary or *condition*, allowing the First to create further things through it. In that case a soul, matter or form might be the first effect, and the bodily counterpart arise thereafter. The philosophers themselves allow multiple effects from one principle under diverse aspects and respects. Finally it has not been shown that a body is a condition for the soul's **productive** action rather than merely its *perception*. If a soul can produce a body without using another body but needs a bodily instrument for cognizing particulars, it differs from a separate intellect defined as independent in both productive and cognitional operations. Thus one cannot simply redefine the soul to make the desired conclusion true.

**Third proof from celestial aspiration.** The spheres are said to move voluntarily, so the object sought is either sensible or intelligible. If sensible, the purpose is attraction of something suitable (appetite) or repulsion of something adverse (anger), both alleged to be impossible for a simple celestial sphere that never passes between disagreeable and agreeable states. Therefore the sought object is intelligible. Its ceaseless pursuit implies extraordinary love (*ʿishq*) and an intelligible beloved. The lover seeks either to attain the beloved's own essence, to attain one of its attributes, or to attain a likeness to it. Direct attainment of the essence or its actual properties would end the motion once achieved; if attainment were intrinsically impossible, perpetual pursuit would supposedly yield despair and cessation, and an attribute of the beloved cannot simply detach and become another's. The desired end must therefore be **successive likenesses** to the beloved, none permanent but each followed by another without limit. Through continuing changes of position the celestial sphere actualizes possible dispositions one after another, so that it acquires at each instant a likeness to its beloved, which is perpetually actual and complete. This beloved is not the single Necessary Existent, they say, because the different movements of different heavens require distinct objects; therefore each sphere has a separate intellectual beloved and there must be several intellects.

The author challenges nearly every entailment. The necessity of unending celestial motion has not been proved. The desire of a sensible thing might concern knowledge or likeness rather than only appetite or anger. Celestial simplicity does not establish sameness in every condition. A desire for something not attained need not invariably cease through despair; the desired object or state might itself be changing and preserved successively, as the philosophers say the desired likeness is. Nor need an intellectual beloved possess *infinitely many distinct perfections simultaneously*; its perfections might be successive. Some objections could be answered, but the whole proof succeeds only if **all** competing possibilities are excluded.

**Second investigation: alleged properties of separate intellects.** Philosophers conventionally enumerate **ten** intellects, meaning at least ten; even they cannot demonstrate that the number is no greater. There is no proof that the celestial spheres are exactly nine: additional spheres might lie between the all-encompassing heaven and the sphere of fixed stars, every individual fixed star might possess a separate sphere, and even smaller subordinate spheres might have intellects governing them in ways known only to God. The familiar scheme obtains ten by making the First Intellect the source of a sphere, its soul and another intellect, the next intellect proceeding similarly, and so on. Nine intellects proceed along with nine spheres, and with the original First Intellect they number ten. The tenth, associated with the lowest celestial sphere, is held to administer the elemental world through the preparations brought about in elemental matter by changing celestial positions. “Administration” by intellects here means efficacious influence and the bestowal of perfections, not the practical governance exercised by a soul through its body.

Further alleged properties are: their eternity, on the claim that every originated thing must be preceded by material preparation and these intellects have no matter; their being individually unique in species, on the claim that multiplication of numerically distinct members of a species requires matter and material individuating conditions; their possessing all possible perfections actually, since transition from potency to act depends on material change and succession; and their apprehension of themselves and all universals. Self-understanding is explained through each immaterial essence's immediate presence to itself, for it would be inappropriate to require a second image of the essence in order for it to understand itself. Other concepts are said to be intelligible together without mutual exclusion. A separate essence free from material conditions is able to apprehend universals; intelligible forms can coexist, and the possibility of their coexistence is conceptually prior to their actually existing together. Since whatever is possible for an immaterial intellect is, on this account, already actual, each intellect must understand both itself and all intelligibles.

The commentator explicitly cautions that these purported consequences depend on **philosophical premises rejected or unproved in kalām**, and thus they should not be read as his own definitive demonstrations. The discussion proceeds to the claim that intellects are sources of celestial motion and further emanations.

Moreover, the first effect need not itself efficiently produce all later things; it might simply be an intermediary or condition, allowing the First to create further things through it. In that case a soul, matter or form might be the first effect, and the bodily counterpart arise thereafter. The philosophers themselves allow multiple effects from one principle under diverse aspects and respects. Finally it has not been shown that a body is a condition for the soul's productive action rather than merely its perception. If a soul can produce a body without using another body but needs a bodily instrument for cognizing particulars, it differs from a separate intellect defined as independent in both productive and cognitional operations. Thus one cannot simply redefine the soul to make the desired conclusion true.

Third proof from celestial aspiration. The spheres are said to move voluntarily, so the object sought is either sensible or intelligible. If sensible, the purpose is attraction of something suitable (appetite) or repulsion of something adverse (anger), both alleged to be impossible for a simple celestial sphere that never passes between disagreeable and agreeable states. Therefore the sought object is intelligible. Its ceaseless pursuit implies extraordinary love (ʿishq) and an intelligible beloved. The lover seeks either to attain the beloved's own essence, to attain one of its attributes, or to attain a likeness to it. Direct attainment of the essence or its actual properties would end the motion once achieved; if attainment were intrinsically impossible, perpetual pursuit would supposedly yield despair and cessation, and an attribute of the beloved cannot simply detach and become another's. The desired end must therefore be successive likenesses to the beloved, none permanent but each followed by another without limit. Through continuing changes of position the celestial sphere actualizes possible dispositions one after another, so that it acquires at each instant a likeness to its beloved, which is perpetually actual and complete. This beloved is not the single Necessary Existent, they say, because the different movements of different heavens require distinct objects; therefore each sphere has a separate intellectual beloved and there must be several intellects.

The author challenges nearly every entailment. The necessity of unending celestial motion has not been proved. The desire of a sensible thing might concern knowledge or likeness rather than only appetite or anger. Celestial simplicity does not establish sameness in every condition. A desire for something not attained need not invariably cease through despair; the desired object or state might itself be changing and preserved successively, as the philosophers say the desired likeness is. Nor need an intellectual beloved possess infinitely many distinct perfections simultaneously; its perfections might be successive. Some objections could be answered, but the whole proof succeeds only if all competing possibilities are excluded.

Second investigation: alleged properties of separate intellects. Philosophers conventionally enumerate ten intellects, meaning at least ten; even they cannot demonstrate that the number is no greater. There is no proof that the celestial spheres are exactly nine: additional spheres might lie between the all-encompassing heaven and the sphere of fixed stars, every individual fixed star might possess a separate sphere, and even smaller subordinate spheres might have intellects governing them in ways known only to God. The familiar scheme obtains ten by making the First Intellect the source of a sphere, its soul and another intellect, the next intellect proceeding similarly, and so on. Nine intellects proceed along with nine spheres, and with the original First Intellect they number ten. The tenth, associated with the lowest celestial sphere, is held to administer the elemental world through the preparations brought about in elemental matter by changing celestial positions. “Administration” by intellects here means efficacious influence and the bestowal of perfections, not the practical governance exercised by a soul through its body.

Further alleged properties are: their eternity, on the claim that every originated thing must be preceded by material preparation and these intellects have no matter; their being individually unique in species, on the claim that multiplication of numerically distinct members of a species requires matter and material individuating conditions; their possessing all possible perfections actually, since transition from potency to act depends on material change and succession; and their apprehension of themselves and all universals. Self-understanding is explained through each immaterial essence's immediate presence to itself, for it would be inappropriate to require a second image of the essence in order for it to understand itself. Other concepts are said to be intelligible together without mutual exclusion. A separate essence free from material conditions is able to apprehend universals; intelligible forms can coexist, and the possibility of their coexistence is conceptually prior to their actually existing together. Since whatever is possible for an immaterial intellect is, on this account, already actual, each intellect must understand both itself and all intelligibles.

The commentator explicitly cautions that these purported consequences depend on philosophical premises rejected or unproved in kalām, and thus they should not be read as his own definitive demonstrations. The discussion proceeds to the claim that intellects are sources of celestial motion and further emanations.

title: The Active Intellect, emanative order, and competing accounts of angels and jinn (vol. II, pp. 51–53)
en:
A further supposed function of the separate intellects is that they **bestow perfection on celestial souls**. The intellect, on this scheme, is the ultimate reason for the sphere's everlasting motion, but does not directly push or govern the body; direct bodily operation would make it a soul rather than an intellect. Instead it communicates perfection to the soul moving the sphere, and the soul receives this influence and transmits an ongoing motion. A material moving power, finite in itself, cannot produce infinitely long motion unless sustained by an intellect whose power is unlimited. The final or **Active Intellect** is alleged to perfect human souls and actualize their intellectual powers, standing to our intellect as sunlight stands to the eye—indeed, more intimately. It is compared to a storehouse of intelligibles: as the soul turns toward it, representations are received; as the soul becomes occupied with sense, they disappear, like the image in a mirror when the mirror is turned away. The soul may receive a different intelligible as it turns toward another object.

They also make an intellect the common proximate source of souls. The Necessary Existent cannot be their direct common source, they argue, because souls exist together with bodies, so multiple effects would issue from the absolutely one First. Nor can material bodies or their forms be the source of incorporeal souls, because material agents act through bodily position and arrangement and do not bring about what lacks position. Nor can one soul be the universal proximate source of all souls, since that is the very explanatory level under discussion. For analogous reasons the proximate source of bodies, considered together, is made an intellect rather than a body, soul or the First. The commentator observes that the argument depends upon several weak premises, particularly that God is a **necessitating cause** from whom only one immediate product may proceed.

**The supposed order of emanation.** The first thing issuing from the Necessary is held to be an intellect. That intellect possesses its own existence, possibility in itself, necessity through another, and knowledge of itself and its source. One account attributes a further intellect to its existence, a soul to its necessity through another, and a celestial sphere to its possibility, assigning the higher product to the higher respect. The second intellect likewise produces intellect, soul and sphere until the celestial series is completed, after which the final intellect administers the elementary world through the changing dispositions of its matter. Another scheme makes the first intellect produce the outermost sphere's matter through its possibility, its substantial form through its existence, its intellect through cognition of its acquired necessity, and its soul through cognition of its original cause.

The philosophers present the mediating distinctions as **a plausible explanatory device**, not as an independently demonstrated mechanical derivation of every level. They do not make existence, possibility and necessity separate independent causes; they are respects or aspects according to which a single efficient principle may be related to several effects. The *Shifāʾ* permits one being to produce one immediate being which then receives additional relational determinations; these subsequent properties can enter into further causal relations, bringing about a plurality whose intermediate conditions were not present in the first production. Separate intellects need not be exactly alike in species or produce the same pattern. The series might end with an intellect responsible for prime matter and the relevant elemental forms, depending on different aspects and the dispositions of recipients. The Necessary Existent, however, is said to be absolutely without such intrinsic multiple aspects, and negative and relational descriptions are known only after other things exist; those descriptions therefore cannot explain the first production of the very others they presuppose, on pain of circularity.

This answer meets a number of objections only by weakening the specific emanative claims: (1) If existence, necessity and possibility are merely conceptual, why could they perform any causal function? If real, why does the original one not produce several such realities? (2) If every intellect produces intellect, soul and sphere, the series must be infinite, not ten. (3) Assigning higher effects to “higher” aspects is rhetorical rather than demonstrative. (4) The fixed-star sphere, containing many stars, and the variety of sublunary forms would require a multitude of effects from one alleged source. (5) If conceptual negations and relations can account for causal plurality, why not use the Necessary's negations and relations directly? (6) If separate intellects can differ in species, so that one ceases to produce further spheres, why may several purely intellectual emanations not occur *before* the first celestial sphere? One cannot establish that the first intellect produces precisely one intellect, one soul and one sphere, or that the intellects equal the number of the major spheres. The philosophers themselves admit additional subordinate spheres and even unknown spheres between the outermost and fixed-star heavens. These hypotheses cannot attain scientific certainty simply through possibility and relative plausibility, especially while resting on the contested axiom that only one can issue from the One.

**Third investigation: angels and other hidden beings.** The topic appears under intellect because philosophers commonly identify **angels** with separate intellects and celestial souls, reserving the term *cherubim* (*karūbiyyūn*) for the entirely separate beings with no relation to bodies, not even by effective action. Philosophers who admit jinn and devils sometimes identify **jinn** as immaterial substances influencing elemental bodies without governing them as human souls govern their organs, and **devils** as human imaginative faculties in their domination over reason, turning the human soul from intellectual perfection toward appetites and sensible or imagined pleasures. Others identify departed human souls as jinn when good and obedient to reason, and as devils when evil, a source of wicked impulses in those still living. The commentator holds that angels, jinn and devils are affirmed by the revealed texts and the broad agreement of religious communities. Reports of encounters with jinn are also ascribed to credible people and saints. One cannot therefore dismiss their existence, but **speculative rational argument alone** does not adequately demonstrate the particular forms alleged for them.

Certain talismanic theorists posit one comprehensive **spirit for each sphere**, subdividing into spirits associated with its parts, as the rational soul governs the human body and possesses distinct faculties in its organs. The spirit of the outermost sphere, which they call the universal soul or greatest spirit, governs its contents and is associated by them with verses about the Spirit and angels standing in ranks or angels surrounding the Throne. They extend the model to spirits of individual degrees of the zodiac, days, hours, oceans, mountains, deserts, human settlements, and types of plants and animals. They connect these claims with scriptural references to angels administering sustenance, mountains, rains, the seas or death. Each type and species is supposed to have its **complete nature** or species-governing spirit preserving it from danger and bringing about characteristic effects. Reports of the vast number of angels are invoked. These claims are attributed and their scriptural proof is not assumed.

**The position attributed to the majority of Muslim scholars** is that angels are subtle **luminous bodies** able to appear in diverse forms, endowed with knowledge and power to carry out arduous tasks, dwelling in the heavens and devoted to obedience. They convey revelation to prophets, continually glorify God and do not disobey His commands. The account of jinn and devils from this theological viewpoint follows at the end of the chapter.
